utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And could we have appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Barney Thomas, April Carter and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good mornings, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. The Defence is today Milos Androvic, Chad Mair, Tina Drolec, Daniela Tasic, and Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just before we start there's an oral decision we'd like to make, but before we do so, I would just want to find out whether the Prosecution has a response thereto. This is the motion of the Defence requesting extension of time to respond to the Prosecution motion about Muhamed Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if I could get back to you on that, on the -- at the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to us hold the reading of the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm sorry about that. I expect the answer is no, we don't respond. But I just want to clear that before -- before the decision is delivered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, we'll wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That being the case, then I call on you Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There is one administrative matter before we start the evidence this morning. The witness for scheduled for tomorrow, Mr. Malik, we were advised yesterday that because of adverse weather conditions en route he was not able to make a connecting flight. He does not arrive now in The Hague until Friday so we will not be able to reach his testimony until the beginning of next week. That -- it's because it's important that we at least capitalise on his presence we would lead from evidence from him as soon as he arrived, but the problem -- the difficulty obviously is that that will not be tomorrow. The witness scheduled to follow him cannot begin tomorrow for two reasons. Firstly, there is difficulty, first of all, in my learned friend Mr. Lukic being prepared. He has commitments this afternoon in another court and he is also wanting to spend some time, I understand, with that witness, after proofing but before the testimony begins and he's currently still under proofing. There's also a difficulty presented to the Prosecution in that the relevant authorities have not yet issued a waiver for this witness but assure us that the waiver will be issued for his testimony on Thursday. So I simply wish to signal at this stage, Your Honours, that we have a difficulty with tomorrow. At the moment we have a witness for today. We don't have a witness for tomorrow. We have a witness for Thursday, and I'm confident that by the end of next week we will have somehow been able to get through all of the witnesses that were otherwise scheduled between now and the end of next week. But tomorrow presents a difficulty. I just wanted to make sure with Your Honours that there was -- that that could be accommodated because if any other alternative arrangements were to be made for tomorrow that would only involve the witness scheduled here for Thursday. And with a -- I don't think any diplomatic efforts can be made to secure a waiver before Thursday because the government is sitting in session on Thursday morning and that's when the waiver is to be granted. So I don't know that anything can be done to speed that up process but I just wanted to bring that to Your Honours' attention at this stage rather than wait until the end of the day today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I -- what waiver are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The waiver --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For who?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: -- is required for the witness currently scheduled for Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: So we loose -- we can't call Mr. Malik for tomorrow. The witness scheduled for Thursday at this stage can't be brought forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying. What I would like to get some enlightenment on is the fact that as long ago as the 29th of April you already notified us that there would be no witness on the 8th, and between that date and the 8th it was not possible to schedule a witness for the 8th?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The 8th, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The 8th of May. According to the schedule that you sent us, on the 8th of May there's no -- well, I must not say you sent us. It comes from Chambers and I don't know how Chambers got it but Friday, the 8th of May, there is -- according to the schedule I have before me there is no witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour, because we're not sitting Fridays yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I thought I had missed something for a moment, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Thank you for that explanation, Mr. Thomas. Is there anything we need to do? The short message is definitely we are not sitting tomorrow. Is that the message?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: That is the message, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You may call the witness for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And that witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. It looks like Mr. Lukic wants to stand up. Okay. Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And I defer to Madam Carter at this point, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. The Office of the Prosecutor calls Dr. Ewa Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ma'am, will you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, will you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I'm Ewa Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What is your area of expertise?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is demography, and in particular demography of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Before we begin the substance of your testimony I would like to go through a few predicate matters. Can you please describe the field of demography?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Demography is a research area that focuses on the population, on the -- describes the population, changes in the population, explains the trends and patterns in demographic phenomena. Among the phenomena there are deaths, there are births, marriages, divorces, and migration. These are the basic demography processes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And you noted for the Court that your specific area of expertise is demography in relation to conflicts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And how does that -- how is that described?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Demography of conflict is a subarea of demography. The main subject of demography of conflict is the demographic consequences of conflict, but in -- within the area also other subjects are studied, like demographic causes of conflict and the similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. We do have your resume through the time of your Galic report. However, can you please the education and training that you have developed regarding this expertise?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I studied statistics and econometrics at the Warsaw Economic University in the 1970s and graduated with the highest grade in statistics and econometrics with a Master degree. Later I engaged in a Ph.D. programme in demography, which I completed successfully, in the area of mathematical demography, also with the highest grade, also from the same university, Economic University of Poland. I worked a number of years at the same university where I taught statistics and demography to undergraduate courses. Later I moved to the Netherlands and became a researcher and later a senior researcher in the Netherlands Interdisciplinary Demographic Institute, which the National Dutch Institute for Demography. And finally, in the year 2000 I joined this Tribunal, the Office of the Prosecutor where the became the head of the Demographic Unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: During your time as an expert have you had the opportunity to testify?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I testified several times -- I think 13 or 14 times before the ICTY Trial Chambers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you name for us which cases you have testified in?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I testified in several cases related to Sarajevo. In the General Galic case, Dragomir Milosevic case. I testified in Slobodan Milosevic, also on Sarajevo but as well on population movements internally displaced persons and refugees. I testified in Prlic which is the Herceg-Bosnia conflict. I testified in Popovic which is Srebrenica. I testified in Seselj and a number of other cases; Lukic and Lukic, for instance, recently; and Vasiljevic, a number of years ago; in Simic et al, which is Bosanska Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: During your time as an expert have you always testified for the Prosecution or have you had the opportunity to testify for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I testified one time for the Defence. It was in Lukic and Lukic case, recently this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. As you are aware -- I have been advised to please slow down so --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Actually it was for me. As you were aware, the reports you compiled regarding the siege of Sarajevo for the Galic and the Slobodan Milosevic cases with the corresponding addendums have been admitted as P2325, through P2331. In today's testimony, I want to focus on the killed and the wounded in the Perisic indictment period, beginning on 23 August 1994. I'd like to begin with the killed. In P2325, your report from the Galic case, at Table A3.13 at e-court page 69, as well as P2331, your report in the Slobodan Milosevic case, at Tables A3 and A4, which is e-court pages 9, you give a monthly break down of the killed soldiers and civilians. These numbers and the totals given do not fully correspond with each other during the overlapping period of September 1993 through August 1994. Can you please explain to the Chamber why these numbers are different?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That explanation for me doesn't -- is not helpful unless I know exactly where we are Madam Carter. You just started talking about the Galic and Slobodan Milosevic cases, and I'm not sure -- and their addendums. Can you refer us to what you are looking at so that if we do have it -- is it in the report of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The Galic report is P2325 and I refer to Table A3.13, and that's at page 69 of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And it is currently on the screen. And, if possible can both pages be brought up, meaning, P2331, at page 9, next to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Carter. Now, what doesn't correspond.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may have one comment, the second table on the right -- yes, that should be replaced by a different one. Yes. This is what we need for our discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have two pages from two different expert reports, both related to Sarajevo. On the left, Table A3.13, this data comes from the Galic report. It is a simple time distribution of killed persons, civilians and soldiers, and individuals with a non-status, shown for the period from September 1992 until August 1995 -- 1994. It's a monthly distribution, so the numbers in the table are absolute numbers of killed persons by month in the mentioned period. This period, September 1992 to August 1994, yes, the period of the Galic report, which is different from the indictment period of this case, and as well, of the period which was discussed in the Sarajevo report that I made with my colleagues for the Slobodan Milosevic case. So, the other page, on our screen, on the right-hand side, comes from the Slobodan Milosevic report. The period of analysis is far broader in this report than in the Galic report. In the Slobodan Milosevic report, we were interested in the casualties of the entire conflict period, starting in April 1992 until November 1995. In the Table A3 which is made for soldiers and A4 which is for civilians the period of analysis is even broader. It begins in January 1992 and ends in December 1995. There is even one more category, unknown month of death included which is the first row in each of these tables. The data shown in the tables A3 and 4 is of the same type as the data shown for the Galic report. It is monthly distribution, monthly distribution of killed persons separately shown here for soldiers and for civilians. Of course, the numbers for civilians are our first interest, so we will be focussing on table A4 from the right side of the screen, and the first column numbers for civilians, from the other table, A3.13. These numbers are not identical, at least we can compare in the period that we can directly compare. There is an overlap between these two periods, and the numbers can be for this period compared. I also prepared a small extract of these data from these two tables for the period relevant for the Perisic case. The period that is 12 months that are the same in the Galic report, in Slobodan Milosevic report and in the indictment of Perisic case. This period begins in September 1993, and lasts until August 1994. I have made a separate table with exactly the same figures and I'm not sure that we can use this table but if we may use this table, then I -- I would like to rather use this because it is easier to see the differences in this smaller sample of data.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were provided with this extract as of yesterday. I did provide it to Defence counsel at that time. It is not on our 65 ter list, so I'm not certain if it would be appropriate to use before us. It is also not on e-court. We can use the ELMO system if the Court would like to review this item and with leave of Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is true that we received this yesterday afternoon. After an information -- informative conversation with Ms. Tabeau, we received several new documents or excerpts from these new documents. I don't have any objection to us seeing them now, but I would like to reserve the right to consult with my client once these documents are translated into B/C/S, because right now they're only in English, and I -- for those reasons I would suggest that we only marked for identification so that I can give our position later on. What I have requested yesterday from Ms. Carter, and she confirmed this, was whether these documents were based on the two earlier reports exclusively and she confirmed that. So if that is -- if it is clear, if these documents are clearer than the ones that we used in the earlier cases, I don't object to them being used here but I would like to be able to review them in detail, but I do agree they be used now and marked for identification for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can use them and we mark them for identification, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, you do confirm that they're based on the earlier reports, exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That is the advice I was given by Dr. Tabeau. I can confirm again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, the graphs that you provided to me as of yesterday, what is the provenance of those items?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: These is a sample of data and results from the two reports that we are discussing now: One being the Galic report on Sarajevo; and one being Slobodan Milosevic report on Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And with the assistance of the usher, we do have the report to be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, on first glance I do note there are some markings, specifically a straight line and a circle, next to the civilians on this chart that is not present in the document that you provided to me or to the Defence. Who made these markings?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I have made them just a second ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You were going to advise the Court as to what -- what created the difference in the numbers of the civilians in these two reports.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Now, first of all, I would like to say that there is a difference in the number of killed persons, both civilians and soldiers, between these two reports, and I'm speaking of the period that is overlapping between Galic report and Slobodan Milosevic report and is part of the indictment, Perisic indictment. This is a period, once again, of 12 months, beginning as shown in this table in September 1993 until August 1994. So these are 12 months that can be directly compared and for each month, the number of civilians and of soldiers can be seen as in this table next to each other. Generally, the number of civilians killed within these 12 months is higher in the Slobodan Milosevic report. It is 548, as opposed to the lower number from Galic report, which is 370. These are the two numbers I have just mentioned, 548 from Slobodan Milosevic, and 370 from Galic report. There is also a difference in the number of soldiers. The difference is less significant. There are 499 killed soldiers reported in the Galic report, and 472 in the Slobodan Milosevic report. So what is the source of these differences? The reports, first of all, were made based on different sources. The Galic report used only one source, Sarajevo Household Survey, that was a special survey run during the conflict by mid-1994 by the research institute in Sarajevo, and we used this one source to compile all statistics in the Galic report. The source is very large. It was a Household Survey that was meant to be complete to cover all households living in Sarajevo by mid-1994. All together 85.000 households were interviewed in this survey. The 85.000 households represented the population of approximately 340.000 individuals. We used this source which we computerised, not all of it, a part of it, by the OTP and established a database, a database that included records of killings, woundings, and natural deaths which we studied in the Galic report. This is a good source but just one source. And when it comes to sources when studying demographic consequences of war, we must be aware of the fact that there is no source which is complete and which is perfect, doesn't have any deficiencies so is also the Household Survey. It was meant to be complete but most certainly incomplete and there are certain deficiencies like incompleteness in data that actually made us exclude certain records from our analysis. In order to improve this situation, in the Slobodan Milosevic report that was made later we have applied a different approach. We worked with a number of sources, big sources, including the Sarajevo Household Survey, which were merged with each other, duplicates were eliminated, overlap was eliminated and one master list of casualties was established. This could only be done for the killed persons, because sources covering injuries and wounding of the population are very infrequent. Sarajevo Household Survey is just one of the few sources that we have in our archive that could be used for this analysis. So in Slobodan Milosevic we worked with a number of sources. It was Household Survey Sarajevo. It was a statistical database on wartime mortality, a big one, established at our request, at the OTP request by the statistical authority of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In this database there are 20 -- approximately 25.000 war-related deaths reported of both civilians and soldiers for the entire country, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and entire conflict period, starting April 1992 until December 1995. Of course, only a small sample of this data is related to Sarajevo. As far as I remember, about 15.000 records in this database relate to Sarajevo. In addition to this databases, we use ICRC List of Missing Persons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you please slow down and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is very difficult for the court reporter to catch up with you. I'm not quite sure because you're talking in English I suspect the interpreters might also be having difficulties, those who are interpreting into other languages. I don't hear any interpretation, I hear you only, but I think -- will you please just slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Of course, I will. I was saying, in Slobodan Milosevic report a number of sources were used together, combined with each other and gleaned from deficiencies. Among these sources there was Sarajevo Household Survey. There was the federal authority, statistical authority database on wartime mortality in Bosnia. There was ICRC list of missing persons for Bosnia and Herzegovina. There a database compiled by an NGO in Bosnia, Muslims Against Genocide. Later this database evolved and became the Bosnian Book of Death, which is quite known in Bosnia as the largest existing database.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If I may briefly interrupt. From looking at the court reporter, I think we're still having difficulty with speed. If you it slow down a bit further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. I'm very sorry. So Muslims Against Genocide is an NGO in Bosnia and Herzegovina which at some point was collecting information about victims of conflict, of civilians and soldiers, and they combined this information in a database on war-related casualties and established a database called Muslims Against Genocide database which we used in this project. So all together, a number of large sources. So sources is the major difference between the statistics compiled in Galic and Slobodan Milosevic report. But not the only difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a question. Do I understand you to be saying, in fact, that your report is the result of you getting information from data that was built up by other people and other organisations. It's not entirely your own work product.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Any report I made is based on sources made by others. So is the Galic report so is the Slobodan Milosevic report. It is -- we are speaking of large numbers of victims of this war, and large number of people worked down there in Bosnia and Herzegovina to put together record of information about these victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking for an explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm just asking whether that is the fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sure Madam Carter will get to the point but I can't wait to hear you tell me about information relating to deaths of civilians and soldiers, and wounded of civilians and soldiers that relates to the period 26 August 1993 to the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that I understood the question. Is the question about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is: I would like to hear what you extrapolate from these reports. I understand that these reports were not drafted for this case. They were drafted for Galic and Slobodan Milosevic. Now, to the extent that they may cover the period covered by the Perisic case, I'm expecting that you're going extrapolate from them and tell us what the figures are relating to the indictment period in the Perisic case. That's what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I suggest we will look at first page from this set of paper that was just introduced this morning. I have included a little table on the first page and this is a table that summarises the number of casualties for the entire indictment period of the Perisic case. That would be -- I could not include the data from the 26th of August but the first month next after it is September 1993, until the end of November 1995. So the overall number of victims is 1.782 and this includes both civilians and soldiers. These are killed persons. The number of killed civilians is 949 and soldiers 833. These numbers come from the Slobodan Milosevic report that I started explaining in terms of sources. This one report actually can be used to extract the relevant numbers for the Perisic case. So that's the number, that's the major information that can be extracted from Slobodan Milosevic report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any similar information regarding the wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there is no information about wounding in the Slobodan Milosevic report. However, this can be extrapolated using the information from Galic report. Based on these 12 months overlapping between these two reports, it is possible to estimate the relationship between killed and wounded civilians and the relationship is some kind of ratio 1:3.2, that means per one civilian 3.2 -- per one killed civilian 3.2 civilians were wounded. So this ratio can be applied and the general number of wounded persons can be obtained for the Perisic period as well. Applying the numbers that we see on the screen. That would be a roughly three times more wounded persons -- wounded civilians compared with the killed civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But I did think that a little earlier you showed us a table that you referred to as absolute numbers but not estimates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The table is absolute numbers and these are counts, that means numbers that can be documented by records, individual records of information about persons. So these are not estimates. And these are minimum numbers, the lowest numbers we have to think of. When it comes to estimation, there is some estimated numbers in the Galic report as well. This ratio I mentioned is not an estimate. It is a ratio that is obtained from the count, from the real data. So the ratio is not an estimate it is the quantification of a relationship --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From absolute figures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from absolute figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But as we know, in statistics once a measure is estimated from the actual data, there can be an extrapolation and the same measure can be applied to a bigger population for which we don't know the same thing. That means I'm speaking here about wounded persons. If there are, of course, good reasons to apply these measures and I think there are good reasons to apply the measure of wounded persons to overall killed number of civilians and obtain an estimated number of civilians for the Perisic period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For clarification of the record, if we can re-call P2325 at page 69. That's Table A3.13. It is already up on the e-court. Thank you. I believe that Your Honour was referring to the chart to the left-hand side and you indicated that we did have some raw data in relation to the wounded civilians -- I'm sorry. I apologise. Actually this is actually for the killed civilians. The wounded civilians would say be A4.13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... or A3.13.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It's Table A4.13, document ID page 02194824.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me? May I have your help, please? Can you help me, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, what we now see before us at Table A4.13 purports to the monthly number of persons wounded within the front lines of Sarajevo and you've compiled the same monthly breakdown. Did you use the same method that you were describing to the Court previously in order to derive these numbers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. These the are the same -- these are also counts of wounded persons. The table comes from the Galic report, so from this table we unfortunately cannot have a figure that would be covering the indictment period of the Perisic case. From this table we can only take the data for one year, beginning in September 1993 until August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. When you indicated that there was a ratio of 3.2, 1:3.2, how did you arrive at that figure?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This figure was obtained using data on civilians from the Galic report, only from the 12 months that overlap with the Perisic indictment period, which is the first year basically of the indictment period, and the overall total of killed civilians was compared with the overall total of wounded persons. It is basically dividing the wounded by the killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: However, you previously indicated that based on that one year, you can extrapolate forward past August 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. It is possible. That -- what can be -- this can be done, indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Is it a normal demographic tool in order to complete these extrapolations?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Demographic extrapolation can be done in many ways, extrapolating this kind of ratio is one way of doing this. There are more sophisticated tools that can be used for this kind of extrapolation. In Dragomir Milosevic report, which unfortunately is not discussed today, another type of extrapolation was presented from which the monthly totals of wounded persons for the entire siege period were obtained by comparison of two sources reporting the -- on the wounding. So a statistical model, more complex model than a ratio was used in this kind of extrapolation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When using that secondary type of operation did you obtain similar numbers to the numbers that you're testifying here today, specifically 3.2 times per every 1 killed?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I don't know for this particular period because I don't have it at hand and I haven't made it. But generally, this model-based extrapolation is even more sophisticated and detailed. That means not only the relationship, the general relationship as the ratio 1:3.2 is contained in this extrapolation but also the monthly distribution or even weekly distribution can be produced using the model. So generally I would think the answer is yes, these kind of ratios are preserved because these are the most general measures, but the more sophisticated the model, the more sophisticated the output of the model.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: But as to a bottom line, as you're sitting here today with the information that you have available, specifically the -- I'm sorry, specifically the Galic report and the Slobodan Milosevic report, can you testify before this Court today that we would be able to use a 3.2 ratio in order to determine the wounded post-August 1994?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I would think yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't want to interrupt, Your Honours, but now that I saw on the screen a technical problem with the translation of this document, this is an official translation made by CLSS which was used already in the Galic case. I'll read it out what it says in B/C/S. It says: A 413, number of persons killed monthly within the front lines in Sarajevo. Obviously this is meant to be a translation of the English version. Unfortunately, in preparing for the examination, I used the English version. I'll try to make use of this fact that I established all the figures are the same, but the heading of the table is completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: My B/C/S is terribly poor. I would not be able to verify or to deny that that fact is accurate. We would ask if Defence counsel could provide for us if there other corrections that need to be made, we can certainly ask for this to be retranslated. But the report was originally drafted in the English and that would be the controlling language of it. But, certainly, we would want to have an accurate record in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, your colleague has indicated therefore that this -- the B/C/S indicates this is the dead [Realtime transcript read in error "date"] instead of the wounded, if you can take that up with your translators, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I will do that at the first opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, given the questioning of the Court as well as the answers that you have provided to me, I have no further questions of you at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just correct the transcript. I don't think this may be corrected later. I said it indicates the dead instead of the wounded, not the date of the wounded. Okay? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you can put this ELMO ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I do apologise for interrupting Mr. Lukic. Given the fact that we are now going back to the item on the ELMO, I would ask that it be tendered as an IC exhibit and marked for identification awaiting translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is an IC exhibit, Madam Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: A court exhibit Your Honour. An in-court exhibit. I apologise, I may use a term that's not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The document -- now, this is the document that is on the screen here? According to my e-court, I have got this one that has got 5090 at the end, which has got -- which is mistranslated, but then there was the previous one. What are you actually wanting admitted, Madam Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're asking for the charts that are on the ELMO not the item that's on the e-court. I believe it is being provided to you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The graphs. Okay. Okay. Fine. These documents are admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2332, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just check with Ms. Carter. These tables that were now marked for identification do not include the additional informative report that we got, the interview made with Ms. Tabeau. You are just tendering the tables, right, and the informative conversation that took place on the 4th of May, 2009, is not part of it, or is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That's correct. We're only tendering the graphs. It is a six-page item beginning with a coloured graph entitled "S. Milosevic Report: Time, trend, and killings."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, good morning. My name is Novak Lukic and I represent the Defence of Mr. Perisic. I will be examining you. A number of years ago, we met in this very courtroom, in the Bosanski Samac case. You may not remember but I certainly do. I will ask you an initial question. I believe it has to do with the methodology. You told this Court that in many cases before the Tribunal you acted as expert mostly for the OTP. You still work for the OTP, don't you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have the chance, did you ever read the decisions of Tribunal in the cases where you were summoned as an expert?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I occasionally do. I read the decision, for instance, related to admitting my reports in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because both you and everybody else here knows that it is the business of an expert to help the Court to arrive at certain conclusions, and that was your role in the cases where you testified, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you interested in whether afterward your report did indeed help the Court to -- to decide in possible future cases that were similar to the one in which you were testifying?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I think, yes, generally, yes, in any case to which a report is relevant, most certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I suppose that you read the decision of the Tribunal in the Galic case, where your report was partly taken into consideration and partly was not.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: If you are speaking of the decision in this case, I -- I don't -- you need to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The verdict of the Tribunal in the Galic case where you were -- testified as an expert, and a part of the verdict reference is made to your report but other parts of your report were not taken into consideration. Did you actually read the first instance decision in the Galic case?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: If you refer to the Judgement, I did read part of it. But it's never the case that a report is accepted as in a whole. There will be results that are accepted and will be deferred to in a Judgement, and there will be parts that are not referred to in a Judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was: If some parts, some comments of the Tribunal, with regard to your report were not accepted, would you be -- would you be inclined to correct some -- those parts of your report by looking for other sources or trying to apply different calculation methods? Was the position of the Trial Chamber some sort of green light for you to try and find something different?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I think, sir, that decisions in the Judgement are justified by numerous factors. It is not only my report that is taken into account but several other factors, like witness testimonies, additional reports, et cetera, et cetera. What you are saying is if there were errors in my report, whether I would be inclined to correct them. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps trying to find another method, another way of arriving at certain conclusions that could assist the Trial Chamber, because the Trial Chamber may decide that Ms. Tabeau's report was not useful to us in certain parts. Well, would that induce to you change something in your -- in your method of work, because there are many similar cases before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Sir, in every next report I make I try to improve things. That is the normal way of doing things for me. I am -- I have been learning, as all of us here in this Tribunal, and I am always trying, in every report, and I do my best to present a good, reliable picture and good statistics. But if you are aware of errors in my Sarajevo report, then please tell me, because, so far, I don't recall that errors were pointed to me by Trial Chambers, which I would need to correct in my next report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not dwell upon that any longer because that is for the Court to decide anyway. A general question: You now -- you now fully stand by your report, both the Galic reports and the Milosevic reports. You stand by the findings and the facts contained in those reports, don't you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But for the Slobodan Milosevic, there is a more recent update, which is the Dragomir Milosevic report, not used in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will focus my whole examination on these two reports that are considered here. So the report from the Galic case and the Slobodan Milosevic case. Do you fully stand by the findings in these two reports? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you about your sources now. I suppose that you agree with me when I say that for any expertise, irrespective of the area of the expertise, it is of paramount importance that the sources of information be of high quality.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The quality of that information presupposes that in your judgement as a researcher they be of the kind that you, as an expert, may trust them. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in your reports, in a certain way, you even assist the quality of the information obtained from various sources that you took into consideration and graded them.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The assessment of sources is an important step in our work. Every source is assessed and various detailed -- in a very detailed way. There are much more information and results from assessment than what is reported in our expert reports because the assessment process is a lengthy procedure and has to do with studying the data items in the database; how deficient they are; how many have empty cells, that means lacking values; how many show logical inconsistencies; how -- what is the coverage every source; what are the biases of every source; whether ethnic groups are well represented or underrepresented or overrepresented. So assessment procedure is a thorough lengthy process. And it is true that there this is an hierarchy of sources that we used in the Galic report which certainly has to do with the reliability and deficiencies of sources, but at the same time as far as I remember, there is a statement in the report that all sources used were of acceptable quality and were relatively reliable. I'm sorry, Slobodan Milosevic report, not Galic report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's correct. You said as much in the introductory part of the Slobodan Milosevic case that all sources have a certain quality and you rank them hierarchically when you couple them to certain events, and I believe that -- this had to do with the army of BiH?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I disagree, it has not to do with the army. The hierarchy of sources was applied to the sources that were used for the master list of victims and not to army records because -- and well, hierarchy of sources was a very practical issue related to the fact that when overlapping records between the sources were found, there was a need to decide which record from which source will be taken first and which ones will be considered to be duplicates. So that was the meaning of the hierarchy. And the lists of military records were not used as part of the master list. They were used for a totally different purpose. They were used for monitoring of the status, military status of victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually it was my error. You said that the report was the report of the federal statistics bureau and that in your report that report had the priority in the hierarchy and not the army report; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The database established by the federal statistical authority was indeed the first priority in our duplicate checks. It is a database that is established by professional statisticians, based on a standardised death notification for every death case. So it has to have a better quality than any other source. All other sources were not compiled by professionals -- professionals, including even the ICRC which is considered to provide highly reliable lists of missing persons. But, still, it is not a statistical authority. They are not professionals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order to draw a conclusion that a certain piece of information is of good quality, I assume that it is of paramount importance that you can compare this information and perhaps find it -- confirmation for it in some other source that this is something that would actually raise or attribute to assessing this as a high quality source of information -- piece of information; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, we cross-references sources all the time, sir. It is a continuous process. This is the major part of the work of my unit, cross-referencing sources through individual matching. We have the population census, as you remember from Simic case, the population census is the core of our population database. We link sources with the population census, compare how information about individuals is reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I wasn't precise enough, but I did not get the answer to my question. The quality of a piece of information, or, rather, a source is better if you can cross-reference the information, if you can compare it with some other information from some other source, rather than if you only have one source of information; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The quality is as it is. The quality of every source is a feature of this source, right? It has nothing to do with cross-referencing which can help the understanding of a given source in a better way. So what you're trying to say that using multiple sources is better than using one source. I hope this is what you are saying. Is that so, am I right or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, here is what I want to ask you, and it has to do with what I have read in your reports. Your assessments -- your conclusions regarding the number of killed individuals in the period that you surveyed, you had several sources for this case. In particular for the Milosevic report, you used five different sources that dealt with a number of individuals killed. One of those sources, for instance, was the source the Federal Bureau of Statistics. Now the quality of the information contained for you was considered to be good, if you could actually find confirmation, or if you could actually compare and collate them with information that you found in other sources, information relating to the same facts.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No. I think you misunderstood the procedure. It is -- the federal statistical authority database is a very good database. But this doesn't mean that all other sources are completely to be neglected. That would be very wrong to understand this, you know, like this. Using more sources is better because the picture is more complete. But using one large source, as the Sarajevo Household Survey, which is huge, really, believe me, it's unbelievably large, there is nothing wrong in using one source and produce minimum numbers from this source. So I believe that numbers in both these reports, Galic report and Slobodan Milosevic report, are very good, and believe me, I have compared my sources so many times, from the Galic report, from Slobodan Milosevic report, from Dragomir Milosevic report, and you would be surprised to see the consistency in trends and patterns obtained from each of these reports. There is a new report in which this comparison is presented. We don't have it here but I know what I am saying. There is nothing wrong in using one source, a single source, like Sarajevo Household Survey, to produce these kinds of statistics. There is nothing wrong to work with merged sources, five of them, seven of them, because the picture is even more complete. The problem with sources on war victims is that they are all incomplete, whether you like it or not. That is how it is. So you either have to work with sources that are showing a good coverage and you know they are unbiased, or you have to work with multiple sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with you, and in that sense, you actually compared sources and assessed their quality. Now my question now is this: Your conclusion and your findings when talking about the wounded individuals, for them, you had -- you used only one source and this is the Sarajevo Household Survey for 1994. Now when these -- when that source is concerned, the information contained therein, you did not compare them with any other sources.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I did. Not in these two reports, but in the Dragomir Milosevic report there is a wonderful comparison with hospital records from major hospitals in Sarajevo, a sample of more than 3.000 records from Sarajevo hospitals related to only civilians and only victims of shelling/sniping and other violent deaths. And there is a wonderful consistency in the trends between wounded persons reported in Household Survey Sarajevo with the Sarajevo hospital records, a consistency that could be used to estimate the overall trend in the wounded persons, both hospitalised and non-hospitalised, not only for the period related to Dragomir Milosevic but to the period of the entire siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know that that is not the subject matter of your testimony in this -- before this Trial Chamber. Now, I said that I will focus all my questions on your findings in the Galic and Slobodan Milosevic cases, which are part of the record, and now I will go back to the same question. In the case of the wounded in the Galic report, because there is no mention of wounded individuals in the Milosevic case, so in the Galic report, did you use any other report other than the Sarajevo Household Survey for 1994? Just answer my question with yes or no. It is simple.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In the Galic report, it is only wounded reported in Household Survey Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that source, for the purposes of that report, you were unable to compare it with any other source in respect of those facts; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In the Galic report, that's no comparison with any other source on wounded persons. Just the Household Survey Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were preparing your report and working on the data, did you, and I mean your entire team that worked on it, did you look for sources yourself or were they offered to you by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No. We looked for the sources ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you try to find certain sources and were unable to get to them, or were prevented from doing so by any authorities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Not that I recall. The source we wanted for the Galic report, Sarajevo Household Survey, was offered to us by the owners of the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you about all the sources from both reports. In view of the fact that most of those sources other than the ICRC and the BiH -- the Serbian Army report and the HVO report, all the other sources are sources whose provenance are the federal authorities, the authorities of the federal Bosnia and Herzegovina, in other words, one of the sides in the conflict. So did you have certain reservations in respect of the authenticity and actual correctness of the information contained therein?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, not really. Why statistical authority would be believed to be biased. Later, I also collected the same database from the RS statistical authority and used these two databases together. So when it comes to Sarajevo, the sources used in the Slobodan Milosevic report were those that were covering the -- these episode of the conflict the best possible way, so that was the major criterion of selecting our sources. If at the time of the Slobodan Milosevic report, of making of Slobodan Milosevic report, I already had the RS mortality database, I would most certainly have taken it and included it as part of my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now just a question that has more to do with your impressions but I believe that you may answer that question, being an expert witness here. Now, during your communication in preparing the reports when you communicated with various institutions, and I mean the Bosnia and Herzegovina institutions who provided the information, was it your impression that they had a vested interest in your producing the report and did they ask you to provide them the report once you have completed it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, indeed, I shouldn't be speaking of my impressions. But, as a matter of fact, it is part of the discussion of sources. You know, I said sources are biased and bias often depends on who makes the sources. As a matter of fact, in every conflict every party in the conflict is interested in showing their victims were the most significant ones. So that is what happens all the time. But this is my role as a statistician, first of all, to recognise the bias, and second, to be able to deal with the bias. And this is what I have been doing. This is what I have been doing in the reports like Slobodan Milosevic. First of all, bias is a very essential issue when it comes to ethnic cleansing, and in the cases of Sarajevo we don't speak about ethnic cleansing. We are speaking of civilians being killed perhaps indiscriminately, so this is a different issue so what really matters are the numbers. The numbers are the crucial issue and from this point of view, in every source all ethnic groups are represented. Every source I used in Slobodan Milosevic case. Sarajevo was multi-ethnic community, as you know, and the Sarajevo part that was under siege was falling under the authority of the federation statistical authority, right? So they were registering deaths of every victims disregarding the ethnicity because is that the role of the statistical authority in every country in every time. So there is no reason to believe that they were selective and they were skipping one ethnic group because they didn't like it. I have no reasons to believe that anything like this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is your position on that the same with regard to the Sarajevo Household Survey of 1994, or when this survey is in question, did you have certain greater reservations before you reached your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Sarajevo Household Survey, again, was meant to cover the entire population that lived within the front lines, confrontation lines in Sarajevo. I believe that possibly because the Bosniaks ran the survey, it was easier for them to get access to the Bosniak families than to minority groups there. But as a matter of fact, as I said, it is not the ethnic composition of victims that is studied in my reports as the most important issue. It is the numbers of victims. It might be so that Bosniak victims are reported more systematically and more completely than other ethnic groups but the other ethnic groups are reported as well in the survey.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this is a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, I would like to continue our discussion regarding sources. Now, the census of 1991, we can agree, was a high-quality source or basis on which you could draw comparisons; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see the federal law, federal code on the census, which was promulgated in 1990, where instructions for conducting the census of 1991 were provided? I believe this was prepared by the then federal statistical bureau.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this census of the population, because of the -- the situation, as it was, the political situation and the sensitivity of that moment, but regardless of that, that in fact the census was very thoroughly and well prepared?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it was prepared very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The census-takers, the individuals who were involved in this, were individuals who had previously been trained - they were especially instructed - in how to conduct the survey?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. There was a training for the interviewers and for the instructors, and a lot of other activities around the census. The preparations took about ten years, as for every census.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the handbooks or the material that the interviewers received in the course of the training provided for certain definitions of certain terms that were to be explored in the census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. But I want to note we are speaking about the most important survey, complete survey of the population in every country. This population survey, the census, is the most essential source of the information about the population in every country as it is complete, it is huge, there is an army of people involved in the preparation and conduct of the census, and after all, it is the major task of the statistical authority in every country to prepare and conduct the census. And, again, I want to make it clear, to avoid any unnecessary discussion, that demographic of war and sources used in the study of conflict and demographic consequences of conflict shouldn't be measure the same way as official statistics. Official statistics and statistics produced in the area of demography of conflict cannot be directly compared because these two situation, like, you know, the time when the census was prepared and conducted and the time when sources on victims of war are compiled, these two situations cannot be compared, because they are totally uncomparable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. So it is your position that they cannot be compared but as a demographer when you assess the quality of a certain source, you have to consider certain standards that in your assessment would be valid when assessing the quality of the source. So we're not talking just about the census but also about war demographics. When you assess a certain source, a source that was relevant for your find information this particular case, for instance, the Household Survey Sarajevo, you used certain standards in assessing the quality of information contained therein and you compare them to the standards -- the world standards, as it were, in compiling such a service; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: You are speaking, sir, of a standard, a standard of assessment of a source. Standards in well established statistical service like the census cannot be taken and applied in war demographics, in sources for war demographics. That is, first, impossible, and second, it would be wrong. One important task of war demographics is first to identify the sources that can be used in a study of casualties of a conflict, to provide a thorough assessment of these sources, to identify deficiencies and biases of sources, and having done all this, to deal with the sources accordingly. So that is my position. So it is not about the standard, worldwide standard of official statistics. It is about the area of war demographics that requires a different approach to sources dealing with sources and analysis. It is exactly the same as you would have said Western countries demography and third-world countries demography is the same; it is not. Believe me, non-Western countries demography is different than Western countries demography, as are war demographics and official statistics. So you can't measure everything with the same standard. That is impossible, and wrong, simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to polemicize here the theory of statistics, but if we have in mind the standards used in Western countries and you compare them to third-country standards, the quality of the statistics is, at the same time, compared with the standards that exist in other countries. Is that correct? Well, just answer me with yes or no. We don't have to elaborate on this.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I can't answer yes and no because you are speaking about standards in western and third-world countries. In third-world country there are no sources as they are in Western countries. In many African countries, for instance, there is no census at all, and still there is a need to have some information about the population, analyse this information and come up with certain meaningful outcomes. So we are speaking of the same situation. We have war demographics that need to be compiled for an area affected by war. That cannot be done using the regular statistical sources and worldwide statistical standards --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, let's narrow that down, let's narrow down our topic under discussion here. You said that you were aware there was law on the census that regulated the census of 1991. Do you remember, and I will tell that you it was Article 21 of the law, of the code, that regulated or provided for sanctions for -- for sanctions for providing false information, so anyone who would provide false information to an interviewer would be punished. Yes or no, do you remember that there was such a provision?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I don't exactly know whether it was 21 Article or something else, but most certainly people were, first of all, obliged to participate in the census, everybody, and everybody by law was obligated to provide the true information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And under the law, every individual was to provide information on themselves. So the -- the basic sentiments of citizens had to be provided by that citizen himself; for instance, the ethnicity or the religious affiliations and so on.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now you're telling us that these two criteria, these two forms that are significant in providing information to an interviewer could not be compared to the surveys or censuses from the time of war. The 1994 census provided for one member of the household providing information for all other members of the household to the interviewer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. However, we didn't use this information in our analysis in Galic. As you might remember, 81.6 per cent of the records of the Sarajevo Household Survey, the part that we computerised for the Galic report which was about 40.000 records, 37.022, 37.022 records, 81.6 per cent of those records were matched with census, 1991 population census. Having done the matching, sir, you can transfer information between sources. So for the records matched you could use the ethnicity reported in the census and this is what we have done. So there is no bias in ethnicity in our report because it is taken from the census, and there is a small group of the individuals that are not matched for which we don't have ethnicity and in our report it says ethnicity unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, and I believe that you also said so during the examination-in-chief, that the many purpose of your report in the Galic case was to establish the number of civilians who were killed or wounded. That was your task, the status -- the victim status was the focus of your work in both reports. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Sarajevo Household Survey of 1994, in respect of the wounded, you, the individuals who compiled this report, there was a -- there was a question relating to the status of a member of the household, whether they were killed or wounded. When I say "status," I mean either this could refer or apply to either a civilian or a military person. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The person giving that information to the interviewer was not obliged to prove the information given to the interviewer by any document when it comes to injury or death, or other status. Whatever was said to the interviewer was entered into the form without any proof or evidence.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. There wasn't -- there was no requirement to prove the facts of death, injury, dates, marital status.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now take a look at this questionnaire. It is part of this document P2325. It's English page 56, and in B/C/S it's page 55. Let us just briefly analyse what kind of information was given or was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could move one page back on the left side. Or, rather, no, leave it this way because the legend is both in B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us start with the following: This is the questionnaire used by the interviewers in the Sarajevo Household Survey in 1994, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is in two languages, B/C/S and English. As far as I remember from your report, you only processed part of the information from that questionnaire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You processed the information from questions 1 and 2. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, among others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we'll get to that. I find number 2 interesting, because it provides information about whether that family household lives at the same address where it lived before the war or if, in the meantime, it had moved to another of the six Sarajevo municipalities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think - and correct me if I'm wrong - that did you not analyse the answers under 4 in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is a question about the members of the family household who had fled or were displaced from Sarajevo or who remained in the territory, as it says, controlled by the aggressor, so that during the population census in 1991, were members of the family household and lived there and, at the time when this survey was made, for some reason, were no longer to be found at that place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you are saying. Well, it is a question that is related to listing the family members of a given household and giving information about whether or not they moved from their original pre-census location. So in this sense, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you separately processed information which I presume were important to you, the answers under 5, 6, and 12. Did I miss anything? 5, 6, and 12, and that is information about casualties and those who died a natural death, including their status. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were drafting the Galic report, this was an important database for you, regarding the status of the victim, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the only other source which also mentioned the status - namely, civilian or soldier - was the report of the burial authority. I believe they were the only ones that had that information.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, you are wrong. There was also the ABiH list of fallen soldiers and other military personnel. That was used in the Galic report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me where in the Galic case you relied on the ABiH report for me to be able to find it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In the executive summary in the most important table, Table 1, in the Galic report, which is page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that table later on.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: We have -- we have two definitions of status listed in this table. The first one is the status, marital status as reported in the household survey. And the second one is called status external definition. It is page 3, English version of the Galic report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the purpose of precision, that is at Table 1 in the Galic report at page 3, right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll get back to that later. But I haven't seen -- oh, yes. Can you tell me where you referred that ABiH source? Is it marked ABiH/VRS?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is the lists of the fallen soldiers, the military lists of fallen soldiers and other military personnel that were provided to us, to the Demographic Unit and for the OTP by the Defence ministries, the ABiH at least by the federal Ministry of Defence and the VRS by the RS Ministry of Defence. So we used these lists in addition to the status reported in the Household Survey, as a more objective definition of the military status, we believed, namely, that the status that was self-reported which was not documented by any formal documents might be an over-reporting of soldiers, and this actual fact is a rather known fact in sever other sources. It is not only this source. People tend to over-report soldiers. So for the distinction between civilian victims and military victims it is really important to have well-reported soldiers on the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree fully that is a very important topic, but I really fail to understand. Maybe it is my fault. When I was reading your report in the Galic case, when I read the content of the report, I cannot see in the content or the report itself that you refer, as you do in the Milosevic case, to a BiH source. I can see you referring to the Household Survey and the database of the Bakije undertaking company, and you analyse those. So my question is: Did you in the Galic report, rely on the -- the report of the Ministry of Defence? Because I haven't seen that anywhere. You mentioned the table, and say that the table considers information from those sources but did you analyse them anywhere? Do you mention that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I just started explaining where in the report you can find references to ABiH list, and Table 1 is just one place. If you go to page 27 of the English version of the report, there is a paragraph, that is the second paragraph for -- from the bottom -- from the top, in which I explain how we used the military lists. Page 27, English version of the report. It's the page where the Table 5 is included and look at the second paragraph and actually the first paragraph from the top is related as well. In this paragraph we explain how the external definition of status was made and from this paragraph you see that we used the records of fallen soldiers through the matching with the census and Household Survey, and we used the records matched for marking them as soldiers, and it was for about 80 per cent of matched records. For the remaining 20 records that were not matched we used the self-reported status. So it is an integration of two definitions. For 80 per cent of records it is the external status from the military lists, and for the remaining 20 records are matched records. It is as reported in the Household Survey Sarajevo, but because it was only 20 per cent of the records for which we used the Sarajevo Household Survey definition, and for the 80, it is the external source used for this definition this item expresses, as a matter of fact, the external definition as obtained from applying the military lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I must ask a layman's question to be able to understand. In any case, generally speaking, in the Household Survey you established that there were no more combatants than civilians who came to harm, based on that information. Or let us take a look at the tables. This will simplify things. Let me ask you this: When you refer to the Ministry of Defence that gave you information about killed combatants, that's the same source that you used in the Milosevic case for the members of the army BiH, or until -- up until 1995 or are we talking about two different sources there?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It's the same source.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll proceed along my way of questioning the status of civilian or combatant; that, I believe, is important to all of us here in this courtroom. But let me get back to the data from the Household Survey. Did the authors of that survey, from 1994, inform you that all households were registered in the territory of the parts of the six Sarajevo municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, they said all to which they had access were registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: About 85.000 households were registered there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
