utterances.text: But neither they nor you were able to tell whether all households that, at the time, were present in the parts of those six municipalities were indeed registered, or do you suppose that, indeed, all households were registered?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I think marginal numbers could have been skipped. But it doesn't matter really. Because 85.000 households is a really huge number if you compare this number from the pre-war data from the census and publications on the households then you see that it is almost all. So it really doesn't matter whether the few you are thinking of were left out or not. That is one thing. Another thing is the numbers we presented in the Galic report are presented as minimum numbers, minimum numbers, at least numbers. So we don't claim it is a complete number that we have there covering all the victims. It is a minimum number. We are aware of the fact that some victims are left out and we even made an estimate to account for those that are not listed in our sources. To address this fact explicitly. So I think all in all what we presented in the Galic report is first coming from a large source, a source that was well prepared, this regarding the difficult circumstances at that time, a source that was collected -- data was collected through interviewers that were trained. It is not that they didn't have any training at all. The structures used in collecting the data were the "mjesna zajednica," the local communities that had a very easy access to the population, so this is all together a very good source and in addition to this, it is large. And we are saying in addition to this, even though it is large and well done, we still believe it is incomplete and we come up with minimum numbers, only minimum numbers, conservative numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would prefer a shorter answer so that we might be able to finish today. I understand that you want to be as precise as possible. But you used this source to statistically establish the population that lived in that territory at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. We tried to estimate the size of this population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You established it by multiplying 85.000 by 4, as the estimated number of members of a household at that time and that territory, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you said yourself that in your report, statistically for the territories of all the municipalities that could be processed before the war, that the overall numbers were raised due to the migrations of population during the period of time in question; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I think the average household size was lower that for -- according to the pre-war data. It was 3 point something, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said a minute ago you did not include question 4 that gave information about the population that had left the territory, in order to get more precise data about the persons who had left Sarajevo in -- during the period in question. You did not consider that, or did you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes and no, I must say. I did not include the data from this questionnaire, but in addition to the main data I used for the Galic report, we at some point collected a pilot sample of the data which was several thousands of questionnaires from two municipalities, I think one of them was Stari Grad and the other one was Centar. And these questionnaires, these pilot questionnaires that we collected were all questionnaires available for these areas and these questionnaires contained data on all demographic events, including the displaced population. So not only killed and wounded and natural deaths were there, but also births, live births and still births, also deaths during the Second World War, and the displaced population living in Sarajevo at the time of the survey. Using the pilot we estimated the displaced population in these two locations within Sarajevo and the number is in the Galic report, and it was about 86 of original population living in these two locations versus 14 per cent of the displaced population in these municipalities. So we had good ideas about the displacement present within the Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That pilot project you analysed encompasses two municipalities, that is about 4.000 households, I believe, and that is .5 per cent of the number of households established, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And according to you, as a demographer, that was a sufficient parameter for you to be able to draw conclusion about the number of persons who had left the territories of those municipalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I have not drawn any conclusions based on this number. I am mentioning this number to you in response to your question. Most importantly, what's the importance, what the meaning -- what's the meaning of the displaced persons? The report is about the number of casualties within the confrontation lines. And if you are leading with these questions to the calculation of rates, then, again, it is irrelevant because rates are calculated only for the population originating from these municipalities and not for the displaced population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, reading your findings, I conclude that the -- your -- the assumed number of persons living there, about 300.000, is the basis that you -- for several analyses of yours. Your assumption of the number of inhabitants of that area is very important, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you simply add up the -- the -- the members of the households in these 85.000 households from the questionnaire? I can't see that this is such a huge task. Why didn't you proceed in this simple fashion?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I think are you wrong about that it is a simple task. It is a huge task. It is a huge task. We are speaking of entering information for at least 300.000 individuals. 300.000 individuals. Do you realise that? In order to have this information that are you addressing right now, you would need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: -- enter all records of both non-displaced and displaced population from this survey, and every questionnaire, and there are 85.000 questionnaires, contains a number of names listed as household members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I must interrupt you. Regarding this information, I believe that the names and personal information are not important. Only numbers are important. And you are saying that merely adding up numbers from 85.000 questionnaires is more difficult than making assumptions the way you did. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, sir, this is not what I'm saying. This is -- what I'm saying is that you have no idea about how statistics are made, how much it takes from the moment a survey --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I must interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I really am soliciting a simple answer. I'm saying that up until the total population, if we rely on the household survey from 1994 as a high-quality source, in a simple fashion, that would take some time. However, could have made -- could have accurately established the population present there, instead of making assumptions. You did not simply count the persons that were -- that could be found in the sources.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I didn't count the displaced persons and the majority of the survey population because I didn't need them. In order to come up with numbers of casualties, of killed persons and wounded persons, I needed to computerise the records of killed and wounded persons and this is what I did, and it really doesn't matter whether a person originally lived in Sarajevo in 1991 or came to Sarajevo from a different part of Bosnia, as long as the person is listed as a killed or wounded person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the figure of 340.000 at which you arrived based on your assumption was used as a basis for your statistical estimate, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: For the estimation of rates, and if you would think a little bit, the 340 [sic] I estimated from the average size of four for a household is more than if you would have used 3 as the average household. And if you think a little bit how the rates are calculated and that the population is actually in the denominator, so the larger size is better for calculation of the conservative rates, that is lower rates, lower, not higher but relatively lower, lower. So what I did I took the conservative approach not to overestimate the rates, which is good for the Defence, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am logically fully aware of what you have said but I don't want to go into the issue of what is good for me or not. I just want to know whether it was statistically correct if you have the relevant data to simply count the persons. You didn't do it. You think that this method of counting people was not -- was not necessary for you, that it was sufficient for you to make an estimate. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, there were two things. It wasn't absolutely necessary, that is one. And, second, it was extremely resource consuming, and I'm not the person to decide about the resources, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. That's an answer. I'll ask you a few questions about another source. With regard to the Milosevic case, that's the ICRC report that you have mentioned, and you consider it a high-quality report, and I understood this to be a report about missing persons which, according to the conclusions of the ICRC, can be used as accounting for missing people, so missing persons that were to be found in their database?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, these are missing persons, not killed, explicitly killed or wounded. These are missing person who are believed to be dead and who died in violent circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And from that source, from that list of missing persons of the ICRC, you matched, as far as I understood, 570 persons who were inhabitants of Sarajevo, according to the 1991 census. Did I understand that correctly? Which means that ...

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I think in order to get the right answer, you, sir, have to go to page 8 of the Slobodan Milosevic report and look at Table A2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In this table - do you have it? - there is a category "Unique ICRC." The Table shows how many records entered per source. So there is a category "Unique ICRC" and it says that 70 records were taken from the ICRC alone. And the number you mentioned, the 570 records have been indeed matched with the census and come from the ICRC, but it is not that all of them are unique ICRC records taken for the Slobodan Milosevic report. The -- another 500 records out of 570 overlapped with other sources, predominantly with sources like Household Survey Sarajevo or Muslims Against Genocide, and were accepted on the basis of the other sources for the analysis. So it is at the same time a proof that the 570 missing persons matched with the census have been confirmed for as many as 500 as deaths in other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I assumed, and my question was, or is, did the Prosecutor inform the ICRC about these 500 individuals that they had on their list as missing persons that they had actually been killed based on other sources. I mean, maybe has nothing to do with our proceedings here, but it seems to me if that's how you matched them, that this is something that would you have done.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to speak about these issues because this is not part of this trial, but we do indeed have an ongoing cooperation with the ICRC and that should clarify your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree. I agree there is no need to go any further into this but this is something that just occurred to me while I was preparing for this cross, considering it useful information. But let's move on to something else. I would like to discuss now the procedure for identifying those killed, and now, let's go to your report in the Milosevic case, the Slobodan Milosevic case. If I understood this correctly, what you did is you matched information from several different sources, and once you matched that information, you actually produced new information or, rather, conclusions that then you incorporated into your report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I didn't produce any new information. I produced a new list of victims and the information in this list, which I call a master list, or integrated list, is exactly the same as in the underlying sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now we will discuss absolute figures, not assessments. So you've, after you have matched the information, you have learned the names, the first and last names, of individuals who were killed. That was one type of information that you matched. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. Names were part of the records matched.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In some sources you also had a very useful bit of information called the pin number for citizens which was very useful for matching; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: You are speaking of JMBG, right? The pin number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in some sources, yes. Predominantly for a number of records in the military lists. But in a majority of sources in Slobodan Milosevic, we didn't have JMBG reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You then received information as to the place of death of that individual, and you established that all these individuals who were the subject of your survey had been killed in those areas of these six municipalities under the BH Army control; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. The place of death was part of the record from mortality sources and was taken for the master list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next type of information was the time of death; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you also had information as to the cause of death or injury; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And finally, perhaps I omitted something, but I am just mentioning here the things that are important to me, the next item was the status of that individual, whether it was a combatant or a civilian.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The status as category is corroborated by the following sources. All the three sources of the three armies: The BH army, the VRS and the HVO, the information provided from those sources. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then, as we saw earlier, you also used, for this category, the Sarajevo Household Survey of 1994, which also included this; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And also the Bakije Funeral Home lists, they were -- the information from that were also contained in the source. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. And I think federal authority also included for a few records, reporting of the military status.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the Federal Bureau of Statistics or the federal Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Federal Bureau of Statistics. But in order to be sure about it, I would have to double-check this. But it wasn't in any case a systematic reporting of the military status in this source.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've -- have also pointed out in your report, and I found this information acceptable but I just want to verify it with you, the lists that you received from the BH army on the soldiers killed, none of those lists contained the information as to the place of their death; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume that you -- that the most reliable source for you regarding this issue of status, whether the person was a combatant or a civilian, was -- or were the military sources; and, for the moment, I would like to discuss the BH army source.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it -- am I correct if I claim that if you found in another source that a person was a combatant but this did not match with the status as provided for in the lists of the BH army, that you would then change that status to civilian, and I'm -- I refer here to those individuals who have been -- who were killed.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Sir, one clarification. The military lists were not used to create the master list as such, because place of death was not reported. Military lists were used for monitoring the status of the individuals that entered the master list based on the other sources used in the project. Whatever record was matched from the master list with military lists, and there were 80 per cent of matched, the military status was assigned as military because the match was established. For a small number of records we couldn't do that because these records were not matched. For these records the status was taken as reported in the source from which the record originated. So it is again a merge here. Basically it is mainly the military status as reported in the ABiH lists, and VRS lists as well, we used those as well, and for a small number of unmatched record it is the status as reported in the original sources. So these are important facts, and we should have a clear picture of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to put a very basic question. If you found based on the Household Survey of 1994 that an individual was listed as a combatant and you didn't find that same person on the BH Army list, what group did you put this individual under in your report in the Milosevic case? When I mean what group, I mean whether you grouped them as -- you put them under civilian or combatant.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: As a combatant. Because he is - or she - reported as a combatant in the original source.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You must know, Ms. Tabeau, that a combatant in an armed conflict is not -- does not imply only a member of an army, a soldier of an army. I assume you know that there is this category of combatant.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware. But as I explained in the Galic report that if a person is reported as a soldier or combatant or whatever way, we just take it as a person who possibly could have died as a combatant. That means in a combat. But we, as a matter of fact, don't know the specific circumstances for death of all people listed as soldiers in any source. So in order to decide whether these people died in combat, we would have to go through these victims on case-by-case basis and study circumstances and then decide. And this is obviously impossible, because the numbers are so large. So what we can do, we can take the status as reported, and we can assume it's a proxy for the circumstances of death, but this is by no means a specific confirmation of the fact that they died in combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact, that fact would have to be verified by the person who compiled the source document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even this person probably is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If at all, yes. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that members of paramilitary units and militias in an armed conflict are not considered civilians? Do you know that this is a category under the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a lawyer but I can imagine that they are not considered, yes. It is not my area, so I wouldn't like to make statements about these kinds of legal issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. Did you by any chance request that the police of the BH provide you are lists of their members killed during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I think the police members are reported in the databases provided by the Ministries of Defence as one of the categories. I didn't explain, but these two databases, or three, we have three databases, one for ABiH, one VRS, and one HVO, these three databases include not only soldiers but also some other categories. They include police members who died during the conflict. They include even the personnel of the ministries of the Defence and associated organisations, and even persons who were part of the production section -- sector providing goods and services for the army. So these are very broad lists and, of course, a large number of individuals included in these lists died as soldiers in -- most likely in combat situations but by no means all of them should and can be seen like this. So police, we didn't request these records separately but police records are part of the databases that we used in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now take a look at your first report, and we've already mentioned this topic earlier but let's now discuss it more thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see document P2325, Table 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is from your Galic report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to avoid any confusion, this P2325, that's a number for the Galic case. It's not an exhibit number for this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is -- it is an exhibit in this case, I'm told. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this is a table of statistical overview. It's called "An Overview of Summary Statistics from the Household Survey Sarajevo 1994." And as regards the individuals killed you established that 1.399 civilians were killed, and 2.381 soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. These are minimum numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on that source?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Based on that source and related to the indictment period only. Galic indictment period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right. When you matched this with other sources, this period, you established that the number of civilians was somewhat higher, the number of soldiers, combatants, somewhat lower, but that the number of soldiers was still greater, far greater than the number of civilians killed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, we can take a look these additional pages which were used at the beginning of my testimony today. I studied these numbers --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I have to ask you based on my prepared questions. Please just answer my questions. I'm just referring to what I have prepared for. So do you agree with me that the number of combatants under both sources was greater, the number of combatants killed was greater than the number of civilians killed in both these sources? So please answer with yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're perfectly entitled to ask questions according to your preparation. I think the witness is entitled to give the answers according to her preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I agree, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So she should be able to go to the documents that will give her the answer that you asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will follow your instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, if you still remember the question, please answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, the number of civilians in the Slobodan Milosevic report for the period of the Perisic indictment, the number of civilians is higher than the number of soldiers killed. I'm speaking of killed persons. But now we can go back to the Galic report and we can pay attention to these 12 months that can be compared between Galic report and Perisic -- and Slobodan Milosevic report, and we can take a look at the table, if you allow me to do so. And in these cases, in Galic the number of civilians will be lower than the number of soldiers, and in the Slobodan Milosevic the number of civilians will be higher than the number of soldiers. So there will be an opposite picture from these two reports. We can take a look at the Table --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of that and that's exactly what I wanted to ask you about. That is what I would like to us talk about here. So let's just talk about the same period of time, just the period of time that you reported in the Galic report, and your findings in the Milosevic case. And perhaps we can proceed in the following manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look -- just a moment, please. Could we now please see the Galic table, A3.13. That will be on page -- just a moment, please. Table A3.13, Your Honours, I wonder if you have a copy of that report before you. This is in Annex 3, Table 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Carter is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Just for the assistance of the Chamber and Defence counsel, that would be page 69 in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you to make a calculation here. But please take a look at 1993 and the number of soldiers, combatants killed. That's in the second column. According to your sources, the sources that you used in the Galic case, in absolute figures, this is the total number of combatants killed in the period from January through December 1993, and I calculated that that figure is 1.389 or thereabout, the total for this. If you have a calculator and if you wish to add it up yourself, I would like to compare this to the same category that you described in the Milosevic case, and I would like to compare this by year. So, according to this table, am I correct that the total number of combatants killed is what we see in column 3, for the period January through December 1993, and we -- if we add them all up, we will get the total number of combatants killed in the Galic case. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In 1993, killed in 1993, combatants, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Soldiers. I would prefer to say soldiers. Is it okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I am using the B/C/S term. You're right, actually. I wanted to check. It is soldiers. That's how it is stated here. Now, I would like to compare the totals that we have here with your table in the Milosevic case, Table A3, where you mentioned the same category, the soldiers except here you use the term "combatant." And in absolute figures for the same territory, the same period you used the figure 1.150 persons. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I don't have these numbers calculated right now, except for this little table that I made for you, actually, to simplify your task. And the total in that table, you're speaking about the same 12 months, I guess, because that is the only period that is the same in these two reports. So what is your total, 1.150 and this is for 1993, entire 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, my total -- correct, that's the period. But when I added up all the numbers in the A3.13 figure without the unknown, all the combatants killed in the period January through December 1993, I came up with the number 1.389. Maybe I'm mistaken but I don't think so. But that number is higher than the number that you have come up with. Even if you look at the breakdown by month, you can see that that number is higher per month in the table that -- in the Milosevic case. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. This is why I insist to show you this table for the 12 overlapping months for Perisic in which we can see these numbers per month. Per month. And you are right, the number of soldiers will be higher in Slobodan Milosevic report, generally. That is what you are saying, and I agree with that. I would like to add that the numbers for the Galic report are the numbers from the self-reported status not from the external definition. This is self-reported in Galic. So we have two different definitions used for data shown in these two reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told me a minute ago that where the status was given -- the status given was different, you accepted the status that was self-reported. Now, why did you -- the status that you -- that was used in the household review -- survey, you -- in other words, let me ask you this: You used -- in the Milosevic case you used the Household Survey of 1994. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Right. But I can answer your question already --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you include all those individuals who were mentioned in that survey as combatants, did you use those figures in the Milosevic case? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: For the remaining unmatched 20 per cent of records. Sir, there are two definitions in Galic, two definitions of status in Galic. All statistics in all tables in the Galic report are presented based on self-reported status taken from the Sarajevo Household Survey. The other definition is shown in the summary table, Table 1, and there is another table, 3, and perhaps more tables only in terms of summary statistics to address the issue of over-reporting the military status by the respondents of the Sarajevo Household Survey which, of course, has impact on the numbers of civilians. But you are comparing two things that are not directly comparable because these are two different definitions of status used in these two reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we are drifting away from each other now. Now my question was very simple, Ms. Tabeau. Please try to answer in simple terms because I'm a lawyer, and I, unfortunately, cannot fully follow your expert report here. The status of combatant or the status of soldier was set forth in the Galic report for a certain period of time, for the same location, where you established that the greater number of combatants were killed in that period than civilians, than the number of civilians killed in that period. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The status in the Galic report is self-reported by the respondents of the Sarajevo Household Survey. So there will be -- if you compare this with the external definition of status, there will be more soldiers, according to the internal definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was my question. According to the source that you used in the Galic case, there was a greater number of soldiers killed than civilians for the reported period; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Compared to the Slobodan Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe on that note, then we can take up from there later, don't you think? We will come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could we please get the second report of Ms. Tabeau back on the screen. That is Exhibit P2325. That is Table A3.13. I said the second report from the Galic case. Maybe I misquoted it. I'm sorry, the first report from the Galic case, P2325.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll return to this table for a little while, Ms. Tabeau. We're now looking at the period from September 1992 through August 1994 in the Galic case report. Do you agree with me that when I say that in the period in question, in all months, except for October 1992, more soldiers were killed than civilians, according to this report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, generally, this is the case. But there will be more cases like October 1992. But generally --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are some. October 1992 and now I see February 1994. But in the other months, and in some months, significantly fewer civilians than soldiers were killed in these municipalities, or parts of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Generally, this would be the expectation that fewer civilians than soldiers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at your report P2331, that is the Milosevic case report, Tables A3 and A4. Let us first agree that we're talking about the same territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Not necessarily, because the territories were, in the Galic report, within the confrontation line, which covered large parts of the six municipalities, and in the Slobodan Milosevic report, these were six -- the same municipalities -- municipalities taken as a whole. So there is a slight difference in the territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh. This is news to me. So you're saying that in the Slobodan Milosevic case, you analysed the territory within the boundaries of the municipalities that were covered by the 1991 census. That is to say, a larger territory than that in the other case.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, slightly larger. We studied the population from the census, 1991 population, for both territories. Using the bridging system between [B/C/S spoken] from the Galic report and the municipalities reported in the census, we were able to establish that the population within the confrontation lines was approximately 80 per cent of the census population. I'm not speaking of geographic territories because that is irrelevant. What is really relevant is the population size in these territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree. But let us make something clear: The population that you examined that lived in the territory in the Milosevic case and the population in the Galic case is 340.000 persons. That is the number. And that's the number that is based on the Household Survey in 1994.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is an estimate of this population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. That means that we're talking about the same number of persons as estimated in both reports.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I'm now confused. Sorry, you -- please rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Galic case, you found out and expressed the opinion that the population was 340.000, based on the 85.000 households that were the source of your work from the Household Survey carried out in 1994, and you rely on the same population size in the Milosevic case report, as the population you are examining.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall that I mentioned the population size. I mentioned six municipalities in the Slobodan Milosevic report, and the population size in these municipalities is not 340.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the population size in those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In -- according to the 1991 population census --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. According to the Milosevic report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is unclear because the population changed since after the 1991 population census and we have the estimate, 340.000 individuals who stayed within the confrontation lines and it is unclear how many stayed outside the confrontation lines. And because of the freedom of movement outside the confrontation lines, it is expected that large parts of the population outside the confrontation lines moved out and separated as much as they could, went far away from the conflict, which is not the case within the population --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- within the population lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now take a look at your report for the Milosevic case, the following table, Tables 2 and 3. These tables show the number of combatants and civilians that came to harm. If we look at the table for the Galic case, for -- which covered the period from September 1992 till August 1994, we saw that in all months there is a greater number of killed combatants than civilians except for two months. Isn't that correct? And if we look at the same months, the same period in these two tables, for each month, if we compare from September 1992, in the same period, we can see that there are more civilians listed here than combatants. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I think -- I agreed already that the number of soldiers will be greater in the Slobodan Milosevic report. Sorry. I'm now confused. Let me think about it. Will be lower. Will be lower than in the Galic report, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In all periods. In all periods, yes. So if you have a particular period in mind, it is most likely correct what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was comparing the two periods that are comparable from two reports. So the same period in two reports reflects different status categories of the persons killed in the same territory. Isn't that so? You have said as much. In the Milosevic case, there were more civilians killed in the same period than in the Galic case.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although you said a minute ago that where the source of your information stated that a person was a combatant or a soldier, respectively, that you stuck to that categorisation. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In the Slobodan Milosevic, it is the military lists, as the main source for the military status. In the Slobodan Milosevic report. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which means that, in the Slobodan Milosevic case, your Household Survey from 1994 were persons were characterized as soldiers, you did not count as soldiers unless they were mentioned in the ABiH report. I'm speaking about the report for 1995. Instead, you reduced the number of soldiers as compared to the number of civilians.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No. We had a long discussion about how this was done in Slobodan Milosevic report. For the matched records we took the military status as reported in the military lists, for the matched. For the matched individuals. For the remaining, it was as reported in the original source. However, it is not that all household records were taken and used as such in the Slobodan Milosevic report, because there was a hierarchy of sources, so most records entered from the federal statistical authority database.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... compare these sources as if they could correspond one to one to each other. They don't. They are -- they don't. On one hand we have a report in which one source was used, Household Survey, and in the other report we have a number of source, large sources used and also organised hierarchically, and there will be differences in reporting in the sources whether you wanted it or not. Our way of dealing the differences in reporting of the military status in the sources was by using one uniform, consistent definition of the military status as reported in the military lists. So this is what we did, and this is a different definition of the status than the definition used in the Household Survey. In addition to this, the number of sources which was bigger, which is another source for differences in the outcoming statistics and there is a slight difference in that territory so there is enough differences not to compare these sources directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Madam, a simple question: Did you, in the Slobodan Milosevic case, discount sources that stated a person as a soldier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has been asked an answered repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have asked the question several times, but I don't believe I got an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have got an answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness has said to you that if the source categorised the person as a soldier, she kept it as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... she's told you that the reason for the difference between the Galic list and the Milosevic list are the following and I may not remember them all. One, in the Galic list, these were self-reported people who tended to over-increase the number of soldiers; two, in the Galic -- in the -- in the Milosevic list, they used soldiers -- army, military lists, not self-reported people; then she said in the Galic report, they went municipality by municipality for the six municipalities. In the Milosevic report they went for the whole municipalities as one single whole, which was slightly bigger than -- than the municipalities in the Galic case. So -- and that's why she is saying -- I see you shaking your head. But if you want, we can look it up in the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I fully agree with your interpretation of the witness's words. But I did not get an answer that would be satisfactory for my analysis. But obviously I cannot get an answer that would be of use to the Trial Chamber, but that is obviously my problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectively to Defence counsel, I point him to page 70, it's beginning at line 11, where she specifically indicates that if it was a matched person from the household list to the military lists, she used the military list. For all of the remainder, she kept the self-reported status. She has been very clear on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. Did I interpret you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very, very correctly, Your Honour. Very, very well. Thank you. I just want to remark that perhaps will be helpful when reading these reports. It is less about directly comparing the statistics from these two reports. It is more about, you know, one report being complimentary to each other. I believe that the Galic report is an important report because it shows unquestionable minimum number of victims and for these victims shows a number of very important distributions, including cause of death distributions in terms of shelling and sniping. It shows sex distribution, age distribution, how many women, how many elderly were killed. It shows municipality, saying where the activities were the most intense. So this is an important starting point. And then we have the Slobodan Milosevic report which is extremely general and gives only overall numbers, but if you read these numbers together with the specific details from the Galic report, then the picture becomes very complete, in my view. There might be a degree of extrapolation which is allowed between these two reports but there shouldn't be a direct comparison of every single statistic between these two reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right, I agree. Just please explain to me where such a difference in categorisation came about, that in one report the number of civilians killed is much greater than soldiers and the other, it's the other -- it is vice versa. So what could have caused such greatly differing results of your research? Because for the same period in two reports you give very different data. What is the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would again object, asked and answer. As the Court has laid out the reasons why, I'm certain that Defence counsel should know as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was trying to explain some of the reasons, but I think you talked to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem, Your Honours, because I don't understand. The witness explained that where the territories differ. That's my problem. I thought that the territorial and -- framework and the time framework were the same, but I understand that -- that the categorisation differs, and Ms. Tabeau says that two reports can be understood as being complimentary but they give a very different picture of the events. However, if it clear to you, I can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is not clear to me but what is clear to me are her explanations, and I was still trying to tell you the differences that she has told us the whole of this morning. One of them was that -- one of them was that -- in addition to what I have told you already, in the Milosevic list there was a multiplicity of sources. In the Galic list, is the HSS list source. In the Galic list, she mentioned the periods, I think, starting from 1992 or somewhere, but then she's -- this was in-chief. But in the Milosevic list, it was for the entire period of the war. Now, these are all factors that one can expect would result in slight differences, in differences. To what extent they affect the differences I do not know. But, you know -- but then, of course, she has just explained to you now that the Galic list categorised according to age, sex --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- whereas the other one is just general. It doesn't give children, women, men, elderly. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I have heard so far today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, in your second report, let us take a look at Table 1A and at Table 1B. That's at page -- it's at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S, it's page 2, and in English it's also page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These are your key conclusions. Let me check if I understood this correctly. In Table 1A you speak about the absolute numbers of those killed. From 1992 through 1995, you state that 3.686 soldiers were killed, and in excess of 3.000 civilians, as direct consequences of the war. Now, these are absolutely numbers that are matched?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I think the number of civilians is 4.015, not 3.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, indeed. 4.015 civilians and 3.686 soldiers. That's what the table states. And these are the figures that you matched from different sources?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then in Table 1B, you work with estimated categories by raising the -- the figures by 24 per cent [as interpreted], as the estimated number of casualties, both civilian and military.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This percentage of 23 per cent [as interpreted], you applied to the population of all six municipalities, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: To the victims from these territories. So, yes, yes, to the victims, to the numbers of victims from these territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've done with this table.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that we agree that the first table contains absolute figures and the second table contains estimates, and it represents, as you said in your conclusion, a -- that this is a -- an inference and it is described how you arrived that inference?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. One is observed, absolute, minimum numbers; one is estimated. That's right. Table 1B is estimated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may ask a question. If 1B is then estimate and 1A is absolute, why do you call 1B corrected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because that is of the method of estimation, it's just a matter of fact a correction for the -- it doesn't have a specific meaning. It is an unfortunate term. It should be called estimated. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A general question that follows from what you have shown us today when you analysed the period of the indictment against Mr. Perisic. If we look chronologically at the number of victims, that number globally speaking has decreased from 1992. It significantly decreased in 1994, and in the three spring months of 1995 it rose but then it dropped again. But generally, my question is: Your survey shows that the number of victims, regardless of their status, drastically decreased from 1992 when the conflict started until the end the war?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I would disagree. I have a very good of chart of this in the set of the materials distributed today in the beginning of this testimony. There is a time trend in killings, on the first page, covering the entire conflict period and we can take a look at this chart on the ELMO. And see all --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can put it on the ELMO, I would like to put Table 1 on the ELMO from your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This first table, or Figure 1, shows in red the oscillation of mortality in civilians and the other, the mortality of combatants. What we can observe is that there is a peak in the first months of 1992 until June, and after that it varies but mostly falls. And the green line represents the period covered by the indictment against Mr. Perisic. If we look at that period until the end of 1995 do you agree with me that this period, globally speaking -- or, rather, that the number of victims globally speaking in that period is significantly below that until August 1995?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes, most certainly. However, there are some local peaks and can you see them in the October 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can perhaps take a look at the table to see that. Maybe the easiest way, because that is what I found when I was preparing for this cross, is to use Table -- you agree with me that each of these peaks, in the period when Mr. Perisic was there, that this highest peak, as it were, was always lower or about the same as the peaks in the previous periods. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On this table, we can see the period in the spring of 1995, between May and August 1995, there is an increased number of victims, both in the civilian and the soldiers' category, and I think that you stressed this in your report, that there was significant surge as compared to the earlier period, a surge in the number of victims, and that can be seen on the Tables A3 and A4.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will now ask you, although maybe this is not part of your expertise, but are you aware that at this time a major BH offensive started, it started in May and went on through May and June, up until August 1995 when the NATO air-strikes began?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this can lead us to the conclusion that the victims, regardless of the category, there is a correlation between the victims and the conflict going on in -- on the battlefields at the time.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't study the factors behind these trends, so, of course, there must be a correlation, there must be an association between combat activities and the number of victims. There is no doubt about it. But I didn't study the causes and especially the military actions of both armies, so I don't think I can answer this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well, fair enough. I would just now like to take a look at one more analysis where the wounded are mentioned, that's in the first report, because that is not the subject of the second report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is table -- in Annex 4, Table 9. I believe that is on page 91, but I'm not sure if that's the same page in e-court. Perhaps page 88. I think that's the right page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's 90, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to know the pages. So page -- that's the first report. Table A4.9, page ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A4.9 is at page 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We discussed a bit earlier, Ms. Tabeau, that the only source for the wounded, and you analysed this only in the Galic report, was the report -- or, rather, information that you received from the survey or census of -- the Household Survey which is the only source that actually also provides information on the wounded; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to make sure that I have correctly understood this category, what you've said here - and that's interesting - you've established that in this period under review, 178 women soldiers were wounded, 2 of whom, as far as I can see, were wounded -- were injured, rather, unrelated to the conflict, but 176 women soldiers were actually wounded in the course of the fighting, correct, during combat, in this period that we are reviewing, which is 1992 through 1994.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Number of women is 178. 178. And they are reported as soldiers, wounded as soldiers. It is the self-reported status.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes. That's uncontested because this is the source that you had, the -- in the Household Survey. Now, in this same report, there is a total of 7.594 wounded men, and I can also see in the penultimate column that there are also injuries and accidents that's unrelated to the conflict. But all the other reports had to -- all the other reported woundings were in correlation or connected to the fighting, to the conflict. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I think there are 36 cases for men of woundings in accident and other cases, including self-inflicted injuries, but honestly, actually it is a very difficult task to decide whether an accident was war related or not. In the Sarajevo Household Survey, many accidents were reported like gas explosions, accidental falls from damaged stairs, accidental falls on street, traffic accidents related to the lack of light regulation of the traffic, and -- et cetera. So personally I believe these accidents were war-related. At the same time I recognise that nobody killed these persons by shooting, by shelling or sniping. But I did include these cases of accidents among the war-related cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And what you have just said, I believe you have also explained this during your testimony in Galic, but that is only an assumption, and what we are discussing here are the figures which was your task to provide certain information based on those figures and not to determine whether the wounding was inflicted out of combat or as collateral damage, because that would be just speculating and that was not your task. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, you are right. I didn't try even to distinguish between collateral and other. However, you must remember that in the Sarajevo Household Survey killed persons are reported separately from natural deaths. All these cases of accidents reported in this table and wounded persons are reported separately from natural deaths, so I believe that -- I have done it right. I didn't mix up, for instance, for killed persons, causes of death of natural deaths with causes of death of killed persons, and for wounded causes of death were reported -- causes of wounding were reported separately. So I have presented the survey data as they were reported. I think I didn't cross any borders here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I will present some of my conclusions based on what we have heard today or what I have read in your reports. First of all, you consider and you stand by both of these reports, and there's nothing in those reports that you feel should be altered in any way. As far as you're concerned, they're completely accurate and properly done, the way that you have worked on these projects.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And your primary task was to try, based on various sources, to determine the number of civilian casualties in the territory under the control of the BH army. When I say "casualties," I mean both dead and injured, or wounded.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, my task was to quantify the numbers of killed and wounded persons, and -- yes. Yes. On the first place. And, of course, show any other details related to these basic numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When determining the status of those individuals, you used various sources, and all those sources confirmed -- or, rather, you used all of those sources for both of your reports to determine the status of those individuals -- or, rather, whether they are a civilian or a combatant soldier?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: So one source, the one from Galic, included the reporting, self-reporting of the status. I used this as reported. And in the other report, in Slobodan Milosevic, I did use the military lists for the determination of the military status. On the first place, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your Milosevic report, you also used the self-reporting, the Household Survey as a source for your report, for your research.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: For a number of unmatched records -- small number of unmatched records the self-reported status from -- well, whatever status was reported in the sources was accepted for the unmatched records. So it is a match. But generally for a majority of records it is as reported in the military lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now I will again go back to what I did not quite understand. In the Milosevic case, did you use the Sarajevo Household Survey self-reporting in -- for in -- in the category status of individual. Yes or no? And I apologise if I'm not perfectly clear again, but did you use that report in the Milosevic case in the unmatched cases, the cases that were not matched with other sources?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then you just used that status, that is, self-reported, there as the status in your reports?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I don't know what to say really, because your problem is that you don't really understand how the -- the micro analysis of data is done. So it is possible that you assign a certain value to 80 per cent of your records and this value would come from the military lists, and there will be 20 per cent of remaining records and you can assign to these records no value but just you can take the value existing in the sources, and that's my answer. This is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, you did use the Sarajevo Household Survey when describing the status, or, to be more precise, you used the Household Survey 1994 in the Milosevic case in determining the status of the victims. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: For a small number of records, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, in the charts that you provided before the Court today, at page 2, you provided for us the overlaps between the Galic reports and the Slobodan Milosevic report. And just so we're clear on what we're talking about --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The differences between the soldiers is 27. There are 27 less soldiers in the Slobodan Milosevic report than there are in the Galic report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That is correct. It is for the 12 months that can be compared between these two reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And secondly, you compared for that one year that were 151 more civilians in the Slobodan Milosevic report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I think the number is 178. 178 for civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Pardon. I actually jumped ahead of myself. So what we're dealing with is we're still -- even taking what it appears that Defence counsel would like us to do in maintaining those 27 soldiers from the Galic report, you still had a net gain of 151 civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. At the beginning of Defence counsel's questioning of you, at page 25, line 14, he stated: "If some parts, some comments of the Tribunal with regard to your reports were not accepted, would you be inclined to correct those parts of your report by looking for other sources or trying to apply different calculation methods?" And you indicated that you had had the opportunity to read some of the Judgements that used your testimony. If I were to hold out to you that at the Galic Trial Judgement, paragraph 581, which has been accepted by this Court as adjudicated fact 130, they indicated that: "The Trial Chamber considers that the main conclusions of the Tabeau report are supported by other evidence in the trial record including evidence tendered by the Defence which shows that the conflict in Sarajevo led to the death or injury of a large number of civilians. The Trial Chamber recalls that the Tabeau report presents minimum numbers from only six municipalities, bearing in mind these limitations, the Trial Chamber finds beyond a reasonable doubt that many hundreds of civilians were killed and thousands were injured in ABiH-controlled areas during the indictment period." Is there anything about this finding of the Galic Trial Chamber that would make you alter your statistics or your opinions?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is only that it is minimum numbers. It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, Mr. Lukic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question in my cross was to a different effect. My question was: If there was a situation where a Trial Chamber did not accept some position of Ms. Tabeau's, whereas Ms. Carter is now here talking about some portions that were accepted by Trial Chamber, so I think that Ms. Carter is now posing questions that are not in line with my cross-examination. And I don't object to Ms. Tabeau answering this question, but I think that is not the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. But the only difference between what you are saying now and what you said when you cross-examined the witness is that now you are saying, If there was a situation where the Trial Chamber did. You didn't put it as a -- as a hypothesis when you cross-examined. You put it as a fact that, indeed, there are some Trial Chambers that did not accept certain parts of her report. That is the distinction between what you are saying now and what you said then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely in that sense that I've said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that same case, in the footnote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter is saying -- is asking the witness, based on the comments that are made by the Trial Chamber in the Galic case, whether there is anything that would cause her, given that comment, to want to alter her report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm clear with what she meant with her question, but my question had to do with -- in the cases where a Trial Chamber did not accept the report, and I think that was the sense of my cross-examination, and that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you did indicate you don't object to Madam Tabeau answer Madam Carter's question. May she go ahead an answer the question? We will understand that you are not on the same page with Madam Carter. Or you say you are not on the same page with Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, do you need me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No. I think my answer is no, I wouldn't change anything in my Galic report, except in the next report I made about Sarajevo I tried to present more complete numbers instead of these very minimum numbers, the absolutely minimum that come from the Galic report. The whole effort was how to improve this, how to present more complete numbers and Slobodan Milosevic is just one of the reports that I attempted to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now as to footnote 2081 from the Galic Trial Chamber Judgement as well, the Court did provide a caveat in which they said: "The authors of the Tabeau report attempted to determine if there was a correlation in terms of timing between the killing or wounding of soldiers and the killing and wounding of civilians." And it concluded in tentative language that civilians were becoming victims of shooting and shelling, not necessarily when soldiers were killed or wounded but this would suggest that the losses of the population were perhaps caused by mechanisms other than those accounting for the killing and wounding of soldiers, and the emphasis was added to that -- the bits that I emphasised in my questioning. Now, I want to draw you to your Slobodan Milosevic report, in which you indicated that you had more complete numbers. If your numbers are accurate, then in 1994, 279 soldiers were killed, while 349 civilians were killed; and in 1995, 307 soldiers were killed, while 350 civilians were killed. Given that the civilians are far outnumbering the soldiers, is this statistically significant to you with regards to the targeting of civilians?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, it is an indication that targeting was possible. But it would certainly require more studying and especially more detailed data by day, not only by month, day, week, decades of the months and certain additional calculations would be needed. A simple thing I could do to investigate this issue is the calculation of the civilian-to-soldiers ratio, which did I, and which is included in the set of materials distributed today on the first page. It is figure 2 and from this chart we can see that there was a number of values of this ratio which indicated that the number of civilians were very close to number of soldiers or was even higher than the number of killed soldiers, so this only confirms that this general observation, the targeting of civilians was possible. Also the correlation calculated for the Galic period overlapping with the Slobodan Milosevic period correlation calculated for monthly data for killed civilians and soldiers shows that these two series were correlated, but if the observation period is larger, then the correlation drops immediately and becomes much lower. So it is possible, that's my answer, but in order to firmly make a statement about this, additional studies of the data would be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That brings us to the conclusion of your testimony, Madam Tabeau. Thank you so much for taking time from your busy schedule to come and testify. I guess you don't have far to go, so you just walk well back to your office --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and you are now excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I turn the floor over to Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I can indicate in relation, Your Honours, to the administrative matter raised this morning, the oral decision, that the Prosecution will not be filing a response. The next witness, as I indicated this morning, will be on Thursday, so we're in your hands now as to whether you wish to dispose of that matter now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Thomas. Then the Chamber will then read -- may the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're back in open session. Thank you so much. The matter stands adjourned to Thursday, the 7th of May, at 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of May, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 16 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
